cues.say: Component six: the queue and workers.
A queue is a to-do list for slow work. Your server writes a note, called a message, and replies to the user at once. Background programs called workers pick up the messages and do the work.
Think of order tickets on a kitchen rail: the cashier doesn't cook.
Why do you need it? After each paid pizza order, the shop sends a confirmation text. The text provider takes one to two seconds, and the customer waits.
Worse, when the provider times out, a paid order shows a checkout error.
With a queue, the API writes one message, text order forty-two, and confirms the order instantly.
A worker takes the message and sends the text. If the provider fails, the message goes back on the queue, and is retried later.
Here's the catch. Delivery is at least once: if a worker is slow to confirm it finished, the queue can hand the same message to another worker.
So jobs must be idempotent: running one twice has the same effect as once. Worker two sees the text was already sent, and skips it.
And a message that fails five times goes to a dead-letter queue, a side list for messages that keep failing. You alert on it.
So what goes on a queue? Anything that can lag a little. Emails and texts,
image processing, like resizing uploaded photos,
and reports or exports, which nobody needs in the same second.
Now a real case. At kickoff, nine hundred orders arrive in thirty minutes. Each one queues a text, and the list grows.
The workers drain it at their own pace. Texts lag a few minutes, but checkout stays instant, and no text is lost.
If the queue keeps growing, add workers. Queue length is the signal to watch.
Here's where it sits: the API writes to the queue, and workers call slow outside services, like text providers.
Two things to know. Save the message in the same transaction as the order, a pattern called the outbox. Otherwise a crash between the two can lose it.
And you don't need Kafka, a replayable log for many readers. A simple queue is enough here.
In the interview, say: at-least-once delivery, plus workers that are safe to run twice.
